stories.headline: Free agents to invest in, avoid during 2026-27 MLB offseason
stories.summary: Here are this offseason's players to target and be wary of, given their projected contracts.
stories.body:
Now that we've projected contracts for the top 50 free agents in this winter's class, let's look at which players could provide the most -- and least -- bang for their expected buck.

In past years, I've done pretty well -- investing in Sonny Gray, Shane Bieber and Shota Imanaga as free agents while avoiding the end of Justin Turner's career and megadeals for players whom teams initially didn't sign to long-term contracts that offseason, like Blake Snell, Pete Alonso, and Cody Bellinger, before they all eventually got those deals.

Last year, my biggest player to invest in was a hit (Michael King), and my five players to avoid combined for -0.3 WAR at over $62 million in salary and over $40 million in future commitments. Now, I'm back again to try to hit the bull's-eye a few more times.

The projected contracts in my rankings provide important context for this exercise, as my choices are based on return on investment -- how I expect the players to perform over the length of their deals at their projected prices.

The rules for this edition are the same I set out for myself last winter: Each group of three players must have one player projected to land more than $50 million, one projected for a one-year deal and at least one pitcher and one position player.

Here are my three free agents to invest in and three to avoid for the 2026-27 MLB offseason.

Free agents to invest in

Seiya Suzuki, RF, age: 32

Projected contract: 4 years, $90 million (22.5 AAV)

Suzuki has been one of the most consistent outfielders in baseball over the past four seasons. Among regular outfielders, he's fifth (behind Aaron Judge, Juan Soto, Ronald Acuna Jr., and Kyle Tucker) in the all-encompassing batting stat wRC+ and 12th in WAR in that span. Suzuki's WAR number drags a bit because his defense in right field had been league average to slightly below, but it ticked up dramatically to plus in 2026. Normally, those results don't hold to the next season for players in their 30s, but it at least sets a higher baseline for Suzuki's decline.

I'm not sure what the high-end market will be for the hitters vying for the second-biggest contract of the winter (behind Tarik Skubal), but Suzuki has a strong case and could get the fifth year and/or crack $100 million. Given his age and position, I think he might come up a bit short, but Suzuki comes with a high floor due to several routes to create value.

When it comes to big-money free agents to invest in, higher-floor hitters with a strong track record of performance and durability are the safest bet, and safety is the name of the game, as obvious values don't exist at this price point. He's very likely to continue playing at a 2.5- to 3.5-win level for the next two or three years, so the risk is just the last year or two of the contract.

Jazz Chisholm Jr., 2B, age: 28

Projected contract: two years, $46 million (23 AAV)

It was a slam dunk that he'd be one of my three "invest" players after I read the market and projected Chisholm to get this contract. Among regular infielders, he's 11th in WAR (11.8, averaging just under 4.0 per season) over the past three seasons, just behind some of the best players in baseball: Bobby Witt Jr., Elly De La Cruz, Gunnar Henderson, Francisco Lindor, Jose Ramirez, Geraldo Perdomo, Ketel Marte, Alex Bregman, Brice Turang, and Jeremy Pena. On top of that, Chisholm is still just 28 and the Yankees didn't extend a qualifying offer to him.

But here are the reasons I think he settles for a short-term deal: His batting average has trended from .256 to .242 to .231 last season, and his strikeout rate has jumped 5% and his 2026 expected wOBA (an all-encompassing hitting statistic with ball-in-play "luck" stripped out) fell to career lows. In addition, his actual wOBA was well better than his expected, so he's trending down in most major categories and also was "lucky" last season. His strong WAR (3.5) is propped up by defensive metrics that some believe don't reflect reality for infielders due to positioning, so you could argue that a DRS-driven WAR (likely in the low-to-mid 2s) is more indicative of his ability.

He is a good bet to get a contract at or near the qualifying offer (one-year, $23.15 million contract), so it would appear the Yankees didn't offer that because they didn't want to risk him seeing a down market and taking the offer to return to the Bronx for 2027. It's hard to quantify exactly why the Yankees feel that way -- I'm sure Yankees fans don't have trouble imagining the reasons -- but Chisholm put up 3.5 WAR this season, eighth among second basemen, in a notably bad season for him. Even if he doesn't improve, he isn't in physical decline and offers lots of baserunning and positional value along with routinely beating his expected hitting numbers due in large part to his speed. So, on a one- or two-year deal for something like the qualifying-offer rate, Chisholm's contract is unlikely to be a heavily negative ROI and clearly has the ability to post a 5-win season if he can make some adjustments; this is something financial professionals call asymmetric risk.

Bryan Abreu, RHP, age: 29

Projected contract: 1 year, $10.5 million

There are a lot of options for this last spot every year, and they are often candidates for pillow contracts, which are one-year deals that can help free agents reestablish their value next offseason. That describes Abreu to a T, along with some other late cuts for this list: Zac Gallen, Daulton Varsho, Trent Grisham and Nick Pivetta (mostly health-based in his case). Two others who got strong consideration were Adrian Morejon, Kris Bubic (not quite enough highly positive ROI potential, but I think both will be worth their contracts) and Hiromi Itoh (limited upside, but also has asymmetric risk). I was considering Evan Phillips before he landed a surprising three-year deal from the Braves.

In Abreu's case, he looked like a potential $50-plus million free agent reliever at this point last year, then had a disastrous 2026 season, when his fastball velocity lost 1.5 mph, slider broke less, walks were way up, strikeouts were down, and he had an almost double home run rate. Because he's still in his 20s and he still struggled with some mechanical and confidence issues this season, there's a clear case that a new coach, a change of scenery and rebuilding his mechanics could help him become his former self as soon as next season.

There's a lot of upside to bringing Abreu back to his former self and not that much downside; I could also see him landing a two-year deal if there are several teams confident that they can fix what ails him.

Free agents to avoid

Randy Arozarena, LF, age: 31

Projected contract: four years, $90 million (22.5 AAV)

Arozarena set a benchmark of 2.5-or-so wins per season from 2022 to 2025, putting up 10.7 WAR over those four years, when it was never below 2.0 or above 3.1. This is relevant because, at age 31 in a walk year, Arozarena put up 5.5 WAR while having top-10 ball-in-play luck in the league, and being below average by any defensive metric in left field.

This means Arozarena is having average luck and also aging similarly to most players, and he projects in 2027 to post 2.0 to 2.5 WAR, without adjusting for more defensive or baserunning decline. If the per-year price will be over $20 million, the team signing him will basically be breaking even in Year 1 of a likely long-term deal, leaving very little room for this to be a good value and tons of room for a disastrous outcome.

Anthony Santander had two straight 2.5ish-WAR seasons, then 3.2 WAR in a walk year at age 30, then -0.9 WAR in the first year of his new deal, and didn't play in the second year. Chris Davis went from a 0.9-WAR season to a 5.4-WAR season in a walk year at age 29, then fell off in historic fashion. Josh Hamilton posted a 4.8-WAR season at age 31 in a walk year, then posted 2.8 WAR for the rest of his career. Teoscar Hernandez posted a 3.4-WAR season at age 31 in a walk year, then put up 1.8 WAR over the next two seasons combined. But that doesn't mean Arozarena will follow these comps, but there's a pattern with spikes in walk years for corner outfielders and/or outfielders in their 30s. There's always demand for middle-of-the-order production and power hitters, so there are always teams willing to take a chance.

Ian Happ, LF, age: 32

Projected contract: three years, $48 million (16 AAV)

Happ is a cleaner "corner outfielder in decline" case than Arozarena, with his WAR dropping (3.7, then 2.8, then 2.6) similar to his wRC+ (121, 116, 107) and similar to his expected wOBA, with a slight head fake into a down year in 2026 (.347, .354, .313). Similar to teammate Suzuki in the above section, Happ also had a defensive improvement in his 30s, but he has been in positive territory for a few years, helped by his arm as well as his range.

That helps Happ's case for a more gentle decline defensively, but he'll likely get a multiyear deal, so he will decline defensively and physically during this deal, and if his hitting doesn't rebound, he might be in a platoon role (he has pretty big righty/lefty splits) where his defensive ability isn't as important in lesser playing time. I feel pretty good about Happ being a starter-level contributor next season, but not far beyond that, so the downside in the projected contract (or even a two-year deal) is paying two times to three times the player's value in the second and/or third year of the deal after not delivering much surplus value in that first year.

Chris Bassitt, RHP, age: 37

Projected contract: one year, $10 million

Bassit gets the edge over some other risky bets, such as Tarik Skubal (the eight-to-10-year deal is scaring off several teams, but he'll be a star for most or all of the front end of the deal), Ryan Jeffers (catchers are inherently risky, and there isn't a ton of upside), and Ty France (he might have been lightning in a bottle in 2026, but he's still decent, especially for a one-year deal for 2027), but each of them project for a solid enough ROI that Bassitt has real potential to be released in 2027 if he can't turn the tides.

Bassitt signed last winter for one year and $18.5 million and was terrible in the first half before missing two months because of a back issue. When he came back, his velocity and results were a bit better, but still below average. He'll be 38 years old in February, and the optimistic pitch for 2027 is that he'll be a version of his post-IL-return self, with a mid-4.00 ERA in a bulk-inning role, but that gives almost no path to success from an ROI standpoint. The signing team would be hoping it all clicks for a 1.5-WAR season in an ideal scenario in which he'd then get moved to long relief or off the roster in the playoffs. But there is also a path to continued decline/injuries and scenarios where a one-year deal could be seen as a bad investment.

stories.headline: MLS wild card predictions: Who will emerge from Orlando-Cincinnati, Seattle-RSL?
stories.summary: The wild card kicks off the MLS Cup playoffs on Thursday, so who will advance to Round 1? ESPN's U.S. soccer analysts make their predictions.
stories.body:
The international break may not be quite over just yet, but in MLS, attention is already returning to the club game. That's because the opening salvos of the MLS Cup playoffs begin on Thursday with the wild-card round.

Having 18 of the league's 30 teams qualify for the postseason might make for a bloated playoff field, but who doesn't love a play-in game? Thursday night will see the eighth and ninth seeds of both conferences square off for a date with the No. 1-ranked side in the East and West.

So, Orlando City vs. FC Cincinnati, Seattle Sounders vs. Real Salt Lake, how will it all play out? Who will advance? Joseph Lowery breaks down the matchups and ESPN's U.S. soccer analysts make their predictions.

Eastern Conference
8. Orlando City vs. 9. FC Cincinnati
Star attraction: There's exactly one outfield player in MLS who's been more transformational than Antoine Griezmann -- and it's Lionel Messi. Among current players with at least 1,000 minutes this year, the FIFA World Cup winner with France is the closest to Messi when it comes to goal contributions per game. Posting a staggering 1.06 combined goals and assists per 90 minutes, Orlando City's star summer signing completely changed their fortunes.

Before Griezmann, Orlando found itself near the East's basement with 14 points in 15 games and a defense hemorrhaging goals. With the former Atlético Madrid attacker in tow, the club's points per game shot up from 0.93 to 1.68, good for the sixth-best tally in MLS since the World Cup break. The Lions are still leaking goals, though -- their 78 conceded this season is tied for the second-most in league history -- but with Griezmann's passing range and goal threat, they truly can outscore their opponents and make some noise.

X-factor: It takes a serious player to nab top billing from Evander, Cincinnati's superstar No. 10, but that's exactly what Griezmann's presence in Orlando has done. Still, both teams will take pains to limit the other's elite creator. While keeping their opponent's star quiet will be a nearly impossible feat for the second- and third-worst defensive teams in MLS, that Orlando City will be paying special attention to Evander will open space for Pavel Bucha.

Outside of Evander and the team's center-back corps, no Cincinnati regular touches the ball more than Bucha. According to American Soccer Analysis, the Czechia international central midfielder takes 8.1% of his team's touches. Bucha's service even prompted manager Pat Noonan to play him as a right wingback earlier this year. Back in the center, the 28-year-old will have a chance to provide the creative touch for the visitors.

Tactical wrinkle: It's all well and good for Cincinnati to have Griezmann at the top of the scouting report and for Orlando to do the same with Evander. Slowing those players down is another matter entirely. How effectively each team accomplishes that task could decide Thursday's match.

Orlando had exactly one true center back in its squad on Decision Day. The Lions have been hurting for quality central defenders, and that pain only increased when Robin Jansson went down with a season-ending injury. Just how will interim manager Martín Perelman compensate for being perilously thin in the back?

Cincinnati, for its part, spent more on salaries for defenders than any other team this year as of the MLS Players Association's May release. Try as Noonan might, defensive stability has evaded his team. They'll need to find another level without the ball to keep Orlando's high-powered attack quiet.

Predictions
Orlando has the luxury of playing at home and will have the best player on the field in Griezmann. Between the Frenchman, Martín Ojeda, Marco Pasalic, and U.S. men's national teamer Justin Ellis, Orlando City's attacking arsenal will be too much for Cincinnati to handle. -- Lowery

Neither of these teams is very good defensively, but Cincinnati seemed to get its act together toward the end of the season. Evander vs. Griezmann should be fun, but I expect Cincinnati to come out on top. -- Jeff Carlisle

You can't overlook the form of Griezmann. He's got nine goal contributions in his past seven games for Orlando and will likely be the difference-maker in this matchup. -- Cesar Hernandez

This match feels more like a Round 1 matchup with MVP finalist Evander taking on Newcomer of the Year finalist Griezmann. Despite two good sides, Orlando should be able to capitalize on the Frenchman's magic to advance. -- Lizzy Becherano

Western Conference
8. Seattle Sounders vs. 9. Real Salt Lake
Star attraction: There was no bigger breakout star in MLS this year than Real Salt Lake striker Sergi Solans. The Spaniard has taken an atypical path, beginning in the Girona academy before heading to Oregon State, being drafted by Salt Lake, going back to school, transferring to UCLA, and now shining in MLS. Solans finished tied for eighth in non-penalty goals (15) during his rookie campaign. So impressive was the 23-year-old that RSL handed him a new contract months into the campaign.

Even with Zavier Gozo's August departure and Diego Luna 's season-ending injury, Solans managed six goals in his final eight games of the regular season. The No. 9 is a workhorse atop head coach Pablo Mastroeni's 3-4-3 attacking setup and it's hard to picture him lasting long in MLS before a European club comes knocking.

X-factor: The Sounders were getting desperate. They'd lost eight games in a row from the middle of May to the middle of August, a streak that seemed unthinkable for a team with Seattle's level of depth and experience. But with a growing injury list and a lengthy barren run, the team needed change. Enter: star striker Dejan Joveljic. In their first notable acquisition involving a transfer fee since Pedro de la Vega joined in 2024, the Sounders spent $6 million in a cash-for-player trade to snag Joveljic from Sporting Kansas City.

Immediately thrust into manager Brian Schmetzer's starting lineup, the Serbia international bagged a brace in his Seattle debut and collected four goals in his first five games. Since then? He's scored just one in six matches. Reliant on service, Joveljic doesn't have the benefit of being surrounded by a consistent or balanced attack. There's a reason his goals have come in bunches, after all.

If the Sounders manage to feed Joveljic on Thursday, they'll put themselves in the driver's seat. If not, the striker's barren run will likely continue as his team's playoff run ends.

Tactical wrinkle: In an underrated pickup, Real Salt Lake signed Canada's starting center back at the World Cup Luc de Fougerolles on loan from Fulham in the summer. The 21-year-old has been tasked with a fascinating role by Mastroeni -- one not dissimilar to how Wilfried Nancy used Steven Moreira during the Columbus Crew 's MLS Cup run in 2023. Constantly encouraged to push into the attack from his right-sided center-back spot, De Fougerolles leads all central defenders with at least 500 minutes this year in passes and touch share in the final third, as per ASA. The next closest true center back to De Fougerolles? Moreira himself.

With the Canadian eager to help RSL overload the attack, Seattle will have its hands full maintaining numerical parity in the back. But if the Sounders can stymie Salt Lake's aggressive possession positioning, they'll have chances to attack the visitors on the break.

Predictions
In the three years of MLS' current playoff format, the lower-seeded wild-card team has won just once in six tries. The odds, then, are in Seattle's favor despite Salt Lake's stronger form heading into this meeting. -- Lowery

The rosters of both teams have been in flux this season, Seattle due to injuries and RSL due to the same plus the transfer of Gozo. But of the two teams, Seattle has the experience to progress, especially in midfield with Hassani Dotson and Cristian Roldan. -- Carlisle

It's going to be a tough one for Brian Schmetzer & Co., but they have enough playoff experience to get this over the line. Keep an eye on Albert Rusnák, who has a goal and two assists in his past two appearances. -- Hernandez

The Sounders went through a difficult season, but Schmetzer's experience in the league can work to out-coach Salt Lake to earn the victory. -- Becherano

stories.headline: Harrison returns to lead overhaul of women's divisional rankings
stories.summary: Here's a look at every weight class to determine the best of the best in UFC, PFL and beyond.
stories.body:
All three women's MMA weight classes in the ESPN divisional rankings have new No. 1 fighters. One of them also has a new No. 2.

The division with the most dramatic changes is women's bantamweight, where Kayla Harrison reclaimed the top spot in her return to the rankings after being ineligible because of more than a year of inactivity. She successfully defended her championship at UFC 334 with a fourth-round submission of another returnee, Amanda Nunes, who had been retired for nearly 3½ years. Nunes is back in the 135-pound rankings as well, at No. 2.

The women's bantamweight top 10 also welcomes Bia Mesquita, who made quick work of then-ranked Macy Chiasson on Saturday at UFC 334. Mesquita makes her rankings debut at No. 9, and Chiasson is out.

Women's flyweight and strawweight acquired their new top-ranked fighters not via returns from inactivity but by inactivity itself. Neither flyweight Valentina Shevchenko nor strawweight Zhang Weili has competed in over a year, so both former champions are newly ineligible. The rest of the fighters in those two top 10s all move up a spot, with the UFC champions in each division, flyweight Natalia Silva and strawweight Mackenzie Dern, taking over as the new No. 1s. Tracy Cortez enters the flyweight rankings at No. 10, and at strawweight, Denise Gomes is newly ranked fifth and Yan Xiaonan is 10th.

The only men's division with changes to the rankings is heavyweight -- but the change does not affect the No. 1 position, where Ciryl Gane remains after successfully defending his title at UFC 334. The man he beat, Josh Hokit, moves up three spots to No. 4 after a resilient showing against Gane. Dropping from the rankings: Vadim Nemkov, who lost for the first time in a decade at the PFL's event in Dubai on Saturday. He dropped the PFL title to Sergei Bilostenniy.

stories.headline: Thomas Frank: Crystal Palace job 'too good' to turn down
stories.summary: Thomas Frank decided the Crystal Palace job was "too good to turn down" after talks with chairman Steve Parish.
stories.body:
Thomas Frank decided the Crystal Palace job was "too good to turn down" after talks with chairman Steve Parish.

The 53 year old Dane, out of work since being sacked by Tottenham in February, has spent the last nine months travelling, spending time with family, and reflecting on his career.

He takes charge of what he believes is an "iconic" English club, but one with plenty of work to do if they want to escape the Premier League relegation battle.

"You know, honestly speaking, I was a little bit, 'When do I want to go back in? Is it now?' Then this opportunity came up," Frank told PalaceTV.

"I was thinking, this is probably too good to turn down for various reasons."

Frank's strong admiration for Eagles supporters -- he was at Wembley when Palace lifted the FA Cup -- was a contributing factor.

He added: "The second part of it was the very good conversation with Steve Parish. He's been around, he knows what's happening, he knows how to run a football club.

"You always say you need to do your due diligence about the one who takes the decisions, and everything I've heard about Steve, everything I knew, it was positive, and then on top of that the conversation with Matt Hobbs, Iain Moody, was big.

"So all that adding up, looking into the team that I see is extremely exciting, good potential, or just thinking, 'Hmm, this is interesting'. And when I'm sitting here, walking around the training ground, it was just, 'Ok, you're back,' which scared me a little bit, but it's good."

That Hobbs and Moody helped convince Frank to sign a two-and-a-half year deal will, for Palace fans, carry hope that the new boss will be backed in the January transfer window.

The Eagles lost a number of key personnel in the summer from their Conference League-winning squad, including Daniel Muñoz to Nottingham Forest and Maxence Lacroix to Chelsea.

Their absence has been felt on a side that has conceded the most goals, 24, in the Premier League.

"To state the obvious, we need to stabilise things," said Frank, who pointed to defending, set pieces in both boxes, and defensive transitions as priorities to address, beginning with Saturday's trip to Coventry.

"We need to bring energy, we need to bring belief, we need to bring confidence, because this is a very, very good team with very good players, but they need to believe in themselves.

"We need to balance a lot of things with aiming high in Europe, two fantastic cup tournaments, but of course the Premier League is the most important if we need to prioritise, but we would like to compete in all things."

- Crystal Palace appoint Thomas Frank as new head coach

- Pierre Sage's shortlived Crystal Palace era was never given any chance to succeed

Frank, who was sacked by Tottenham after a run of only two wins in 17 matches, said he needed to "re-energise" after that disappointment.

He travelled to Japan and Australia with his family, spent a rare summer in Denmark, reflected on a relentless decade of work, and started speaking to people to get inspiration.

Then, Palace called.

"Timing is everything in football," Frank added. "Coming back to the convincing conversation with Steve, Matt and Iain convinced me that this was the right time to come back."

stories.headline: NHL Tonight: Keys to Capitals-Lightning, 10 other Tuesday games
stories.summary: Find game previews, betting intel, broadcast information, stats and highlights here.
stories.body:
It's another packed schedule in the NHL on Tuesday night, with 11 games on the slate.

That includes a 2024 and 2025 Stanley Cup Final rematch in Florida, two old-school Southeast Division foes squaring off, and an early preview of the Stadium Series.

Read on for a look at what you need to know for each game, including betting info and broadcast details.

Odds are provided by DraftKings and subject to change.

Los Angeles Kings at Boston Bruins

7 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | BOS -148, O/U: 6.5

As recently as Thursday, the Bruins were in first place in the Atlantic Division, but two straight losses has them beginning play on Tuesday in fourth.

It's a good time for the Kings to be on the schedule, as L.A. is seventh in the Pacific and enters this game on a four-game losing streak of its own.

These two clubs squared off on Oct. 17 in SoCal, a 4-1 win for the Bruins in which four different players scored a goal.

Artemi Panarin missed the Kings' game on Saturday for personal reasons, and his return is eagerly awaited given that he leads the team in both goals (eight) and assists (11) this season. On the other side, captain David Pastrnak tops the Bruins' leaderboard in both goals (nine) and assists (17) as well.

Edmonton Oilers at Florida Panthers

7 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | FLA -112, O/U: 6.5

The Oilers have been rolling of late, currently riding a five-game winning streak. Connor McDavid continues to power the offense, and he's currently on pace for 203 points by season's end. (Bookmark ESPN's McDavid Tracker!)

But Tuesday night he faces the Panthers, who beat McDavid and the Oilers in the finals in 2024 and 2025, so perhaps they have a psychological edge here.

Greg Wyshynski identified this matchup as one of his Games of the Week:

"Animosity still runs deep between these two, who met for the Stanley Cup in back-to-back seasons. ... But from an Oilers' perspective, this will be a solid early test for a team that has been one of the NHL's best so far."

Columbus Blue Jackets at New York Islanders

7 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | NYI -135, O/U: 5.5

The Blue Jackets and Islanders have been among the wild-card contenders off and on for the past few seasons, and their results thus far in 2026-27 are indicative what can happen when one team wins the draft lottery while the other hasn't picked first overall since 2002.

Matthew Schaefer -- the player selected with the No. 1 pick in 2025 -- was instantly impactful for New York, unanimously winning the Calder Trophy last season and leading the team in assists (15) and points (21) this season. The Jackets are still waiting on 2024 first-rounder Cayden Lindstrom (No. 4) and 2025 first-rounder Jackson Smith (No. 14) to make their NHL debuts.

Columbus enters Tuesday night on a four-game losing streak, while New York has won its last two.

Buffalo Sabres at Philadelphia Flyers

7 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | BUF -118, O/U: 6.5

Teams in playoff position at Thanksgiving stay there around 77% of the time by season's end. And with that date coming up soon, these two 2026 playoff teams are in a bit of peril.

The Sabres are sixth in the Atlantic Division with an 8-8-4 record, and come into this game on an 0-3-1 stretch. The Flyers are 6-11-6 and have alternated wins and losses the past five games.

Philly took the first game in the season series between the teams, 3-1 on Oct. 21. Perhaps the team that wins this one starts a streak to get back among the wild-card contenders (at least).

Ottawa Senators at Winnipeg Jets

7 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | OTT -120, O/U: 6.5

The Jets are one of the hottest teams in the league right now, riding a six-game winning streak that is bookended by games in which they came back from 4-0 deficits to win in OT or the shootout.

The Senators aren't quite that hot, but have won four of their past five (and earned the loser point in OT in the fifth).

The two teams are about even overall on offense; the Sens have scored 3.14 goals per game to the Jets' 3.10.

The matchup could come down to the men between the pipes. Winnipeg has gotten pretty good play -- all things considered -- from Stuart Skinner and Nico Daws, but Ottawa has Linus Ullmark, who is the NHL leader in goals-against average (1.47) and save percentage (.939).

Washington Capitals at Tampa Bay Lightning

7:30 p.m. ET (Disney+/ESPN+/Hulu) | TB -162, O/U: 6.5

After two straight losses to the divisional rival New Jersey Devils, the Capitals are hoping for better luck against their old Southeast Division rivals in Tampa.

The Lightning took the first game in the season series 3-1 way back on Oct. 3. Erik Cernak, Anthony Cirelli and Brayden Point are all on the injury report, but this game is listed as their estimated return date.

One factor that will help the Capitals in this game and beyond is for Alex Ovechkin to get out of his slump, as he has scored just one goal this season. Ovechkin has scored the fourth-most goals in his career against the Lightning (51 in 87 games), behind the Thrashers/Jets (58 in 77), Flyers (54 in 83) and Hurricanes (53 in 98).

Toronto Maple Leafs at Chicago Blackhawks

7:30 p.m. ET (TNT) | TOR -142, O/U: 6.5

Well, there have certainly been higher points in the Original Six rivalry between the Leafs and Blackhawks. Toronto holds a 295-268-100 edge in the teams' all-time regular-season series, but Chicago won the most recent playoff series in the 1995 conference quarterfinals.

Neither team made the 2026 playoffs, and each is last in its respective division heading into Tuesday.

The good news is that these games between two struggling teams can be a fun watch, and that's doubly true with the amount of star power in the mix here. Toronto's Auston Matthews is in the midst of a bounceback season with 12 goals and 17 assists through 22 games, while Chicago's Connor Bedard leads his team in assists (11) and points (17) despite missing six games.

Anaheim Ducks at St. Louis Blues

8 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | STL -135, O/U: 6.5

Save for a couple of off nights against the Preds and Isles, the Ducks have taken flight as of late, winning six of their previous eight games.

Cutter Gauthier is a big reason why, as he enters this game on a nine-game goal streak (16 total during the span), which is the longest by any NHL player in 29 years.

He is chasing down the franchise record of 11 straight games with a goal, set by Teemu Selanne in 1997.

The Blues don't have any skaters riding any such streak. But goaltender Joel Hofer has been leveling up this season right before our eyes. The 26-year-old has a 2.28 GAA and .921 SV%, both among the top 10 in the league.

Nashville Predators at Minnesota Wild

8 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | MIN -192, O/U: 6.5

The Wild are on top of the Central, with elite players at forward (Kirill Kaprizov, Matt Boldy), defense (Quinn Hughes) and in goal (Jesper Wallstedt). Minnesota won the first game in the season series between these teams, 3-1 back on Oct. 1, and has just two losses (both in OT) in its past 11 games.

Despite a loss to the Sharks on Sunday, the Predators are another of the NHL's hottest teams of late, having won the prior seven games, and they have charged into third place in the Central. That streak included wins over elite Cup contenders like the Lightning, Hurricanes, Avalanche and Golden Knights.

Can they knock off one more Tuesday night?

Dallas Stars at Vegas Golden Knights

10 p.m. ET (TNT) | VGK -135, O/U: 5.5

By a weird quirk of the 2026-27 NHL schedule, these two teams will meet in consecutive games against one another (Tuesday, and again Thursday), and then their only other game will be played outdoors: the 2027 Stadium Series game at AT&T Stadium in Arlington, Texas.

Both teams entered the season as playoff returnees, and it would be shocking if either missed the 2027 postseason. So consider this game (as well as Thursday's) a precursor not only to the Stadium Series at Jerryworld, but a potential Western Conference finals preview, too.

The superstars are delivering for both teams. Dallas' Jason Robertson has 10 goals and 12 assists through 20 games, while Mikko Rantanen has nine and 13. Vegas is led by Jack Eichel (nine goals, 18 assists), Mitch Marner (three goals, 23 assists) and Mark Stone (11 goals, 10 assists).

Calgary Flames at San Jose Sharks

10 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | SJ -125, O/U: 6.5

After some major struggles, the Sharks might be starting to figure things out. They've won three of their past four and are just a point back of the Mammoth for the final Western wild card (with a game in hand).

The rebuilding Flames are three points back of San Jose, but are proving to be the latest example of a "fun bad team," whether it's goals for/against, excellent Hometown Remix unis, or the occasional viral postgame quote from Devin Cooley.

Sharks superstar Macklin Celebrini is the player to watch in this game; a three-point outing against Nashville on Sunday gave him 11 in eight games this month.

Reminder: Fans can catch all the action in the NHL streaming hub and on the ESPN App.

As noted above, the Maple Leafs and Blackhawks have played a lot in their shared time in the NHL. As it turns out, Nov. 17 is a good date for them to be playing again.

Why? The first meeting between the franchises was exactly 100 years ago; on Nov. 17, 1926, the Chicago Black Hawks hosted the Toronto St. Patricks at the Chicago Coliseum, with the Black Hawks winning 4-1.

The St. Patricks were sold in 1927 to Conn Smythe, who renamed them the Maple Leafs after the national symbol of Canada -- excellent marketing strategy!

The Black Hawks became the Blackhawks in 1986, when it was discovered that their original NHL contract used the compound word -- after 60 years of using two words for the team name. (Yes, really.)

stories.headline: What the NBA's first month has revealed about all 30 teams
stories.summary: With the season's first month nearly in the books, Ben Golliver examines the biggest storyline so far for all 30 teams.
stories.body:
The NBA season is a month old, which makes this a natural time to take stock of all 30 teams.

The San Antonio Spurs, Los Angeles Lakers, Philadelphia 76ers and Boston Celtics sit atop the standings, the defending champion New York Knicks are treading water, and several aspiring contenders are juggling star injuries.

And even though Thanksgiving is still more than a week away, the Oklahoma City Thunder have already executed a rare early-season trade and the New Orleans Pelicans have already fielded a public trade request.

With so many developments to wade through, here's what we've learned about all 30 teams since opening night.

Jump to a team:

ATL | BOS | BKN | CHA | CHI | CLE

DAL | DEN | DET | GS | HOU | IND

LAC | LAL | MEM | MIA | MIL | MIN

NO | NYK | OKC | ORL | PHI | PHX

POR | SAC | SA | TOR | UTAH | WAS

Atlanta Hawks
The first month revealed ... Kingston Flemings is a great fit

To no great surprise, Hawks coach Quin Snyder opened the season with a starting lineup -- Nickeil Alexander-Walker, CJ McCollum, Dyson Daniels, Jalen Johnson and Onyeka Okongwu -- that boasted a phenomenal plus-20.3 net rating in 391 minutes in 2025-26. That decision, which favored experience and continuity, left 2026 lottery pick Flemings and offseason trade acquisitions Luguentz Dort and Aaron Wiggins as reserves.

But Atlanta's starters weren't nearly as potent on offense in the early going as they were last season, so Snyder rejiggered his lineup by replacing the 35-year-old McCollum with the 19-year-old Flemings after only eight games. Atlanta's starters have played at a faster pace and boasted a stingier defense since the move, albeit in a small sample size.

Though Flemings is unlikely to generate Rookie of the Year buzz with several of his draft classmates posting huge numbers, he should be in the All-Rookie mix because he already has distinguished himself in a veteran-dominated rotation with serious playoff aspirations.

The No. 8 pick fits Atlanta's blueprint perfectly: He's confident on the ball but doesn't overly dominate possessions, he can space the court with a dependable outside shot, and he's a pesky defender who thrives in an up-tempo style.

Boston Celtics
The first month revealed ... there is life after Jaylen Brown

Boston's blockbuster summer trade of Brown to Philadelphia for Paul George was met with shock, sadness and anger in some corners of the Celtics' fanbase. Brown stoked those hard feelings last month by playing up the tension with former teammate Jayson Tatum: "There's no beef, but it might be a little lamb chops and some gravy."

Unfortunately for Brown, he played like Hamburger Helper in his first game against his former team last week, a blowout victory for the Celtics. Though that high-profile showdown wasn't representative of Philadelphia's strong start, it was further proof that Boston has moved on smoothly after the breakup. As of Tuesday, the Celtics boast the East's best offensive rating and point differential.

The Celtics haven't skipped a beat without Brown because the 36-year-old George is playing his best basketball in years. The nine-time All-Star forward is a natural fit in Boston's 3-point heavy offense, and he's outperforming Brown in several advanced metrics, including win shares and player efficiency rating. George's health will be a key factor in whether Boston can maintain its torrid pace, but he already has helped his new fanbase find joy after the abrupt ending to a beloved era.

Brooklyn Nets
The first month revealed ... the hole in the middle needs addressing

There's a glass-half-full argument that the Nets aren't as hopeless as they appear. Forwards Julius Randle and Michael Porter Jr. are established impact players, and young guards Mikel Brown Jr., Egor Demin and Nolan Traore offer enough glimpses of potential to sustain a beleaguered fanbase.

But it's tough to buy the optimism as long as the Nets are stuck with such a gaping hole in the middle. After trading longtime center Nic Claxton to acquire Randle this summer, Brooklyn has tried to get by with career backups Day'Ron Sharpe and Moritz Wagner. That plan isn't working: The Nets rank 24th in defensive rating and have already suffered four losses by at least 15 points.

If the losing continues, chatter will mount that Brooklyn should be sellers at the deadline to gather assets for the future. But the Nets might be better off bucking conventional wisdom by investing in a midseason upgrade at center to give Brown, Demin and Traore a chance to develop in a more functional environment. Given that Brooklyn must swap its 2027 first-round pick to Houston, why not take a shot?

Charlotte Hornets

The first month revealed ... the post-LaMelo offense is atrocious

The Hornets rank 30th in offensive efficiency, but even "dead last" dramatically understates how inept they've been since trading LaMelo Ball to the Timberwolves over the summer. Though Charlotte theoretically takes a modern approach by leading the NBA in 3-point attempts, their 102.5 offensive rating harkens back to a previous era. In fact, no team has performed that poorly since the 2015-16 season.

Still, this is a pretty obvious "buy low" opportunity. In addition to trading Ball, Charlotte has been without injured guards Kon Knueppel and Coby White. Remove three key ball handlers from any team's offense, and things are bound to fall off a cliff. Sion James, a 2025 second-round pick, is in over his head as a stopgap starter. It won't be this bad forever.

Getting Knueppel back healthy is the top priority. The 2026 Rookie of the Year runner-up has logged only six minutes this season because of hamstring injuries, and his ability to function as a scorer and connector will make life easier for everyone around him. Forwards Brandon Miller and Naz Reid have struggled to score efficiently without high-level guards to create quality looks, and Charlotte's limited centers have gone missing in the dysfunction.

Chicago Bulls

The first month revealed ... Caleb Wilson can't catch a break

Imagine watching the latest Avengers movie in theaters, only for the action to keep getting interrupted by commercial breaks. That has been the aggravating story for the high-flying Wilson, who has suffered three hand injuries since February.

Chicago's No. 4 pick was off to an intriguing, if uneven, start before fracturing his right hand on Nov. 11. The 20-year-old forward averaged 18.9 points -- third in his rookie class -- and dunked 20 times in his first 10 games. During his best moments, Wilson has looked like a future franchise player for a rebuilding Bulls organization that desperately needs one.

Is Wilson injury-prone or just unlucky? For now, it seems like terrible luck. His freshman season at North Carolina was cut short by a pair of unrelated injuries: a broken bone in his left hand and a broken right thumb. Wilson's latest injury also appeared to be a fluke as he banged his hand while reaching for a steal against Spurs center Victor Wembanyama. Thankfully, Chicago expects its thrilling rookie to return in four to six weeks after undergoing surgery.

Cleveland Cavaliers
The first month revealed ... ownership isn't getting its money's worth

Cleveland's $208.9 million payroll ranks eighth this season, but the franchise has already guaranteed more salary in 2028-29 and 2029-30 than every team except the Thunder. In other words, owner Dan Gilbert is all-in financially when it comes to competing for a championship.

How's that going? The Cavaliers are hovering just above .500, and they're not getting the return on investment they were seeking from a pricey starting lineup. James Harden, Donovan Mitchell, Peyton Watson, Evan Mobley and Jarrett Allen combine to make nearly $180 million this season, yet they have posted an atrocious minus-12 net rating through eight games.

Though the 37-year-old Harden is showing major decline to start the season, nagging fit issues among Cleveland's longtime core players remain unresolved. Kenny Atkinson is facing renewed hot seat chatter, but this appears to be a team that needs to change some key players -- and unload some expensive contracts -- rather than dump the coach that guided a 2026 Eastern Conference finals run.

Dallas Mavericks

The first month revealed ... Cooper Flagg is the real deal

Every check-in on the Mavericks is an excuse to gawk at Flagg's progress. The 2025 No. 1 pick is averaging 23.5 points, 6.7 rebounds and 6.2 assists in his age-20 season, numbers matched by only LeBron James and Luka Doncic at the same point of their careers. Flagg is firmly on track for his first All-Star selection, as he ranks in the top 25 in both player efficiency rating and win shares.

Predraft analysts were enamored with the old-school flavor to Flagg's game, and he's certainly doing his best to bring the midrange shot back into fashion. Though he has struggled to find his touch from beyond the arc, Flagg has compensated by shooting 62.5% on midrange jumpers. (For context, Kevin Durant's career high from that distance is 59.1%.)

But Flagg's best virtue is his nonstop motor: He leads Dallas in steals, deflections and distance covered per game, and he sets a competitive tone despite being the team's youngest player. As a result, the Mavericks should remain a factor in the West's play-in tournament race if they can maintain their defensive improvement from last season.

Denver Nuggets

The first month revealed ... Aaron Gordon has become a drag

Gordon boasted a 19.5 player efficiency rating during the Nuggets' 2023 championship season, the highest mark on the team besides Nikola Jokic. The do-everything power forward was in his prime at age 27, and his energetic help defense and finishing made him a perfect complement to Denver's MVP center.

Fast-forward to this season: Denver no longer profiles as a top contender, in part because the 31-year-old Gordon looks like a shell of his former self. Gordon's player efficiency rating has plummeted to a career-low 11.1, and he's shooting a career-low 41.3% from the field. Denver is really missing his presence around the basket: Gordon averaged 2.6 dunks in 2022-23, but the former dunk contest standout is down to fewer than one per game this season.

Denver's offense, which ranked first in 2025-26, has slipped to 10th without a more reliable third option to support Jokic and Jamal Murray. Meanwhile, the Nuggets' longstanding depth concerns have become more difficult to mask with Gordon struggling.

There's no easy offramp for the front office because Gordon's contract is on the books through 2028-29 with an average annual value of $36.4 million.

Detroit Pistons
The first month revealed ... Duncan Robinson has been a lifesaver

The Pistons deserve credit for hanging tough despite a challenging early schedule and the loss of starting center Jalen Duren to a hamstring strain. Cade Cunningham has already led Detroit to quality wins over Boston and Philadelphia, and he poured in a career-high 52 points against Washington last week in an MVP-caliber performance.

Cunningham's efforts are no great surprise, but few could have predicted Robinson's emergence. The 3-point marksman has raised his scoring average by more than five points, has shot 43.1% on 9.1 3-point attempts per game and posted a team-best plus-7.6 plus-minus. Somehow, the 32-year-old forward, who went undrafted in 2018, has been one of the league's most improved players.

The Pistons should treat Robinson's strong start as a well-timed blessing rather than a long-term solution to their scoring woes. Ausar Thompson has stepped up as a secondary playmaker and Duren will provide a boost once he returns, but Detroit still needs more pop to keep pace with the league's best attacks and improve on last season's second-round showing.

Golden State Warriors

The first month revealed ... Yaxel Lendeborg is the Rookie of the Year favorite

Coming into the season, it was easy to discount Lendeborg's chances of winning Rookie of the Year. After all, the Michigan product turned 24 in September, was picked outside the top 10 in a strong draft and joined a veteran Warriors team that missed the 2026 playoffs.

Ready-to-go role players on mediocre teams don't typically fare well in the Rookie of the Year race, especially when they are almost five years older than the top one-and-done prospects.

But Lendeborg has shattered all expectations by averaging 20.8 points, 7.4 rebounds and 3.4 assists for the surprising Warriors, who are off to a winning start despite Stephen Curry's oblique strain. The 6-foot-9 forward not only leads his class in win shares, but he has set his sights on becoming the first rookie to earn an All-Star selection since Blake Griffin in 2010.

Elgin Baylor, David Robinson and Malcolm Brogdon all won Rookie of the Year at age 24. In addition to that precedent, it's worth noting that Lendeborg has held his own among the league's best young players regardless of draft class. Only two players on winning teams are younger and average more points than Golden State's rookie: Victor Wembanyama and Flagg.

Houston Rockets
The first month revealed ... less Kevin Durant is more

Fred VanVleet's return from a knee injury that sidelined him for the 2025-26 season has provided a noticeable boost to Houston's offense. After ranking eighth last season and sputtering out in the first round, the Rockets are up to second in 2026-27.

Though VanVleet has helped restore Houston's structure, coach Ime Udoka has shifted some responsibility from Durant to Alperen Sengun. The Turkish center leads the Rockets in scoring, assists and shot attempts, while Durant is averaging a career-low 13.6 shots. The two-time Finals MVP didn't even sacrifice this much when he was flanked by Stephen Curry and Klay Thompson in Golden State.

So far, this looks like a healthy adjustment. The 38-year-old Durant struggled with turnover issues when asked to take on extra playmaking duties in VanVleet's absence, and last season's Rockets never found a reliable framework for finishing close games. Houston has already accumulated quality wins over the Spurs, Thunder, Celtics and Nuggets, suggesting its new balanced attack will hold up better in the playoffs.

Indiana Pacers

The first month revealed ... there's no plan without Tyrese Haliburton

The Pacers spent all of 2025-26 patiently waiting for Haliburton to return from an Achilles injury, only to watch their franchise guard suffer a hamstring strain just four games into this season. Though Haliburton's latest injury is much less serious, the impact of his absence on Indiana's offense has been nearly identical.

After Haliburton led a top-10 offense and carried Indiana to the Finals in 2024-25, the Pacers' attack fell to 28th last season. And since Haliburton went down in October, the Pacers have ranked 25th on offense and stumbled to a 3-7 record. Starting center Ivica Zubac is off to a disappointing start after arriving via trade from the Clippers last February, and his struggles are emblematic of a wider identity crisis.

The Pacers painstakingly constructed a roster intended to make the most of Haliburton's playmaking and cover his defensive shortcomings. Though Pascal Siakam, Andrew Nembhard and Zubac are all talented players, they're not capable of keeping the train on the tracks without their conductor. Haliburton still has time to come back and salvage a winning season, but the clock is ticking.

LA Clippers

The first month revealed ... Darius Garland isn't a one-man band

The Clippers appear headed for their first losing record since 2010-11 because they've shed too much scoring talent over the past 12 months. The trades of Kawhi Leonard, James Harden and Ivica Zubac were bound to take a bite out of LA's offense, but injuries to Brandon Ingram and Bradley Beal have forced Garland to assume the heaviest burden of his career.

The results haven't been pretty. Garland, a two-time All-Star, is averaging a career-high 4.9 turnovers, and he has the worst plus-minus on the team. Opposing teams have cranked up the ball pressure against the Clippers' undersized backcourt, and Garland has made crucial giveaways during several second-half collapses already this season.

Ingram's return can't come soon enough: Garland needs another shot creator to balance the offense, and forwards Rui Hachimura and Derrick Jones Jr. don't possess enough dynamic scoring ability. On the bright side, ageless center Brook Lopez has been fabulous during an otherwise dismal opening month.

Los Angeles Lakers
The first month revealed ... Luka has never been better

The Lakers have feasted on a cupcake schedule thanks to Doncic, who has been merciless in his first season in Los Angeles without LeBron James. The Slovenian guard is averaging career highs in points and player efficiency rating, he's leading the NBA's most efficient offense and he's on track to become only the third player in the 3-point era to post a usage rate above 40.

Doncic was brilliant throughout most of his six-plus seasons with the Mavericks, but he has reached a new peak when it comes to commanding game flow. The six-time All-Star has reoriented his game away from the basket area to take advantage of his soft shooting touch from all ranges. Rather than barreling through low-post traffic, he's now more likely to twirl, stop or fade into a jumper from just about anywhere on the court. It goes without saying that he can still punish extra defensive attention with his exquisite vision.

Entering the season, Lakers coach JJ Redick said his biggest question about his team was how it would handle adversity after making so many roster changes over the summer. That remains an open question. Unlike many leading contenders, the Lakers have avoided significant injuries to their core players and have skated to one of the league's best records as a result. For now, Doncic and Wembanyama have separated themselves from the pack in the MVP race.

Memphis Grizzlies

The first month revealed ... Ty Jerome was ready for the green light

Memphis has cooled off since its 6-0 start, but Jerome continues to deliver All-Star-level production as a late-blooming scorer. Before joining the Grizzlies two years ago, the journeyman guard's claim to fame was finishing third in the 2025 Sixth Man of the Year race as a member of the Cavaliers.

But the Grizzlies handed the keys to Jerome after trading franchise cornerstones Jaren Jackson Jr. and Ja Morant, and the 29-year-old guard has responded by averaging 25.4 points and posting a 23.1 player efficiency rating. Remarkably, those numbers rival Morant's best years in Memphis.

Though Jerome sometimes hunts shots a little too enthusiastically, it's hard to argue with the results given that he's leading a top-five offense while earning just $9.2 million. The post-Morant Grizzlies are tracking toward a postseason appearance in the first year of their rebuild, which is no easy task in the loaded Western Conference.

Miami Heat

The first month revealed ... Giannis Antetokounmpo is back

The Heat's 0-4 start led some corners of social media to declare Antetokounmpo's South Beach era was already doomed. A different, less catastrophic story has emerged in recent weeks: Antetokounmpo has bounced back from a lost 2025-26 campaign to become one of the league's most productive stars, and his supporting cast has gradually settled into sensible roles.

The Heat's roster construction still leaves a lot to be desired, but the 31-year-old Antetokounmpo has reasserted himself as a high-volume scorer who still has enough raw power and quickness to collapse defenses. The 10-time All-Star ranks second in dunks despite Miami's spacing concerns, and he's powering an offense that has climbed to eighth.

There's enough going well for Miami to feel comfortable about its playoff outlook. Guard Davion Mitchell has been superb as a ballhandling guard, Klay Thompson has enjoyed a late-career renaissance and coach Erik Spoelstra smartly removed the listless Andrew Wiggins from his starting lineup. But Antetokounmpo's unorthodox pairing with Bam Adebayo remains a point of concern. The star big men have a modest plus-3.0 net rating when they share the court.

Milwaukee Bucks

The first month revealed ... past mistakes are haunting them

If any team could push a button to magically wipe its roster and salary cap sheet clean and start fresh with an expansion draft, it would probably be the Bucks. It has been hard to judge the first year of the post-Antetokounmpo era because mistakes from that period continue to cloud the picture.

For starters, Milwaukee is stuck paying Damian Lillard more than $22.5 million per year through 2029-30 after waiving and stretching his contract in 2025. Myles Turner, the starting center whose arrival was supposed to appease Antetokounmpo, is coasting through what's shaping up to be the worst season of his career. And Kyle Kuzma, another trade acquisition from Milwaukee's frantic patchwork efforts, is averaging a career-low 11.3 points.

The list goes on: Gary Trent is barely playing after signing a four-year, $64 million contract, which is subject to an NBA investigation as possible payback for allegedly signing below-market deals to join Antetokounmpo's supporting cast in 2024. To make matters worse, former coach Doc Rivers said in a recent interview that Antetokounmpo was "not easy" to coach and "doesn't necessarily have this super IQ." How is new coach Taylor Jenkins supposed to build a team for 2027 and beyond when the franchise seems paralyzed by its past?

Minnesota Timberwolves

The first month revealed ... Tim Connelly is the Executive of the Year favorite

Connelly has never won the award despite building contenders in Denver and Minnesota, but this is shaping up to be his moment. The headline move was a bold trade for polarizing guard LaMelo Ball, who has reset a once-moody locker room.

Though Ball and franchise guard Anthony Edwards demonstrated instant chemistry, Connelly's ability to reinforce his backcourt rotation paid major dividends when Edwards was sidelined by knee surgery in late October. Ball has kept Minnesota's offense afloat, and Ayo Dosunmu, a savvy 2026 trade deadline addition, has raised his game as a stand-in starter.

Even Connelly's late-summer flier on Jonathan Kuminga has proved worthwhile, with the forward providing quality minutes as a complementary option. With former Timberwolves Julius Randle and Naz Reid off to forgettable starts on new teams, Connelly's moves look even better in hindsight.

New Orleans Pelicans

The first month revealed ... Dejounte Murray won't be missed

The Pelicans have only themselves to blame for Murray's recent trade request. By making no major roster changes to a team that won 26 games last season, New Orleans set itself up for another season of aggravating losses and hard feelings. Murray, the team's most accomplished guard, couldn't even make it to Thanksgiving before asking out and being sent home.

The good news for New Orleans is that Murray's departure helps solve one of its key roster dilemmas. Murray and 2025 lottery pick Jeremiah Fears were clearly a poor backcourt fit, and they posted an abysmal minus-11.3 net rating in 148 shared minutes. Fears will benefit from a larger role and more developmental minutes, and Murray's departure will enable coach Jamahl Mosley to surround the undersized Fears with bigger lineups.

Murray's trade request was a poor decision: The Pelicans were 1-8 with him in the lineup this season, and outside suitors won't need to look hard to find video evidence of his poor body language and mounting frustration. The 30-year-old guard sat out most of the 2025-26 because of an Achilles injury, has appeared in one playoff win since 2018 and is on the books for $32.8 million. This could take a while.

New York Knicks

The first month revealed ... the magic is gone

During their 2026 championship run, the Knicks epitomized the idealized version of basketball in which five guys come together to form a seamless group, and each player is essential to winning. The 2026-27 Knicks look like a more normal modern team: Stars Jalen Brunson and Karl-Anthony Towns are producing, but it's not clear whether they have enough reliable help.

Crafting the chemistry needed to win a title is hard; maintaining it is arguably even harder. Mikal Bridges and Josh Hart, two returning starters, have both looked lost to open the season, and the Knicks' bench, which ranks 25th in scoring, isn't potent enough to pick up the slack.

New York's performance in clutch situations has also been alarming: The Knicks, who were 6-3 in 2026 playoff games that were within five points in the final five minutes, are just 2-6 in such games this season. That sharp swing is a reminder of how difficult it will be to reproduce the death-defying fourth-quarter comebacks that fueled the Knicks' championship run.

Oklahoma City Thunder
The first month revealed ... the camel's back is broken

There's something very admirable about the Thunder maintaining a winning record and a top-five defense despite losing seemingly half of their roster to serious injuries. But the more time that passes since Jalen Williams, Cason Wallace and Chet Holmgren went down in quick succession, the harder it gets to believe Oklahoma City will still be a contender come playoff time.

The Thunder's offense has slipped to below average without Williams and Holmgren, the second- and third-leading scorers on their 2025 championship team. Shai Gilgeous-Alexander's efficiency has taken a noticeable hit due to these key absences, and Oklahoma City has struggled to generate enough 3-pointers to keep up with the league's best offenses.

Loyalty has been a guiding principle throughout the team's time in Oklahoma City, but it will be put to the test if the Thunder can't recover from their rash of injuries. With Gilgeous-Alexander, Williams and Holmgren all under contract through 2030-31, the Thunder lead the league in long-term salary commitments and are staring at massive second apron penalties as soon as next season. How will Sam Presti work out of this jam?

Orlando Magic

The first month revealed ... not much

With all due respect to first-year coach Sean Sweeney, the mediocre Magic are mired in a depressing déjà vu. Paolo Banchero and Jalen Suggs are injured again, Orlando's offense is stuck below average for the 15th straight season, and a decent defense isn't quite good enough to pick up the slack.

Though it's hard to pinpoint genuine progress, Franz Wagner is flourishing in Banchero's absence. The German forward, who sat out more than half of the 2025-26 season because of injury, has bounced back by averaging 24.2 points, 6.8 rebounds and 8.3 assists. That should give him a shot at his first All-Star selection, even if Orlando's record continues to lag.

The Magic should be pleased with Anthony Black's growth, and backup forward Tristan da Silva has helped space the court as a high-volume 3-point shooter. But unless its fortunes radically improve, Orlando will be forced to consider breaking up its high-priced core of Banchero, Wagner and Desmond Bane.

Philadelphia 76ers

The first month revealed ... they're not actually a superteam

"Superteam" is one of those designations that gets tossed around a little too loosely in the rush of offseason excitement. Though it's tempting to use superteam as shorthand for any star-studded roster, it really should be reserved for juggernauts such as the 2016-17 Warriors. Standards are important.

The 76ers have been very good, but they haven't cleared the superteam bar because it's too easy to nitpick their stars. Joel Embiid is averaging career lows in points and player efficiency rating, and his 3-point shooting has been so poor that it feels like a tribute to former teammate Ben Simmons. LeBron James has had some nice performances, but his night-to-night inconsistency has served as a reminder that he's turning 42 next month.

On the bright side, Philadelphia has come together more quickly than expected. James' teams often need a month or two to get on track after his arrival, and the 76ers are already sitting atop the East standings thanks largely to their 10-0 record in clutch games. Give a healthy chunk of the credit to electric guard Tyrese Maxey, who is tied for second in clutch scoring leaguewide and could be headed for a top-five finish in MVP voting.

Phoenix Suns
The first month revealed ... Jalen Green's breakout has been canceled

Plenty has gone wrong for the Suns during a rough opening month, but Green's declining play is probably the most troublesome development. The 24-year-old guard is averaging career lows in points, shot attempts and player efficiency rating, and his dreadful minus-19.2 net rating is easily the worst mark on the team.

No one would watch this version of Green and believe he was selected ahead of Evan Mobley and Scottie Barnes as the No. 2 pick in 2021. The Rockets smartly moved him in the Kevin Durant trade, and the Suns have been unable to squeeze any meaningful value out of an explosive guard who struggles to make 3-pointers, get to the free throw line and consistently defend.

Green is on the books for $36.3 million this season, and his $36 million player option for next season could complicate his potential trade value. Regardless, Phoenix must be honest about his lack of development and consider benching him in favor of more useful contributors.

Portland Trail Blazers

The first month revealed ... Damian Lillard and Deni Avdija are an exceptional match

Lillard has been on an endless quest to find the right co-star ever since LaMarcus Aldridge left the Blazers for the Spurs more than a decade ago. Portland tried pairing Lillard with CJ McCollum in an explosive backcourt, but the small guards were a bit redundant and encountered difficulties in the playoffs. Then, Lillard joined Giannis Antetokounmpo's Bucks in what felt like a failed corporate merger of two very different brands.

After returning to Portland and recovering from an Achilles injury, Lillard is now cast alongside Avdija, a dogged playmaking wing. The Blazers' stars share an underdog's competitive spirit, and they have fashioned quick chemistry thanks to their complementary offensive games. Though Lillard now does most of his damage from beyond the arc, Avdija prefers muscling through the paint for layups and free throws.

Despite losing Ja Morant to a hamstring injury after only four games, the Blazers have sailed along thanks to an elite offense powered by their new-look duo. Lillard and Avdija have posted an excellent plus-10.2 net rating when they've shared the court this season, and both have played well enough to deserve serious All-Star consideration. Will they become the first pair of Blazers selections since Lillard and Aldridge in 2015?

Sacramento Kings
The first month revealed ... Darius Acuff Jr. is the NBA's most fascinating experiment

There's a natural inclination in the analytics community to look at how the Kings are deploying Acuff and uncork a solemn head shake of disapproval. After all, the 20-year-old rookie point guard is launching nearly 23 shots per game on subpar efficiency, committing piles of turnovers and earning a reputation as one of the league's worst defensive players. The Kings rank in the bottom five on both offense and defense, and they will be hard-pressed to win 15 games this season. How is this the plan?

Sacramento backed itself into this dark corner by trading both Tyrese Haliburton and De'Aaron Fox, and its ability to retool has been severely limited by the negative value contracts of Domantas Sabonis, Zach LaVine, De'Andre Hunter and Keegan Murray. The hot seat talk is already swirling for coach Doug Christie given Sacramento's 1-12 record, so praying Acuff can develop into a star is the best of their terrible options.

Acuff is certainly a flawed young player, and there's a spirited debate to be had about his upside as a 6-foot-2 guard who looks as if he will always be a defensive liability. With that said, Sacramento's decision to turn him loose isn't his fault, and he has displayed an impressive fearlessness in the face of so much dysfunction. Until this roster is overhauled, let Acuff keep shooting to his heart's content.

San Antonio Spurs

The first month revealed ... the Spurs should win the 2027 title

Fresh off a series of Finals collapses, San Antonio pump-faked critics by trotting out a new four-guard starting lineup and promptly losing its first two games of the season. Since then, the Spurs have steamrolled through a soft patch of the schedule for 12 straight wins.

And that questionable starting lineup? It has compiled a plus-33.9 net rating and helped San Antonio rank in the top four in both offensive and defensive efficiency. The key to the group is Victor Wembanyama, whose impact and production have been slightly masked by the fact that he's playing fewer than 30 minutes per game. It's no wonder the 7-foot-4 center keeps producing Wilt Chamberlain comparisons: He's averaging 34.6 points, 14.0 rebounds, 4.0 assists and 5.2 blocks per 36 minutes and posting a preposterous plus-29.5 net rating.

With Wembanyama stepping forward as the NBA's most dominant player and Oklahoma City's injuries opening the door for him to make a return trip to the Finals, San Antonio should be viewed as the undisputed title favorite.

Toronto Raptors
The first month revealed ... Jakob Poeltl has been a weak link

The Raptors are reeling without Kawhi Leonard, having lost eight of 11 games since the two-time Finals MVP was sidelined by knee swelling. Toronto sits outside the top 10 in both offense and defense, and all five of its wins this season have come against teams with losing records entering Tuesday.

Toronto's frontcourt depth has been an issue. Poeltl, a veteran center, is barely treading water in his minutes and was benched by Raptors coach Darko Rajakovic on Sunday. When Poeltl sits, Rajakovic turns to smaller lineups featuring Collin Murray-Boyles that can be overwhelmed by traditional centers or offenses that prioritize attacking the paint.

Poeltl's shortcomings are especially problematic because the Raptors gave him a four-year, $104 million extension in 2025. That deal will be difficult to trade, and it could also complicate Toronto's efforts to add depth at center. Once Leonard returns, his sheer talent should help mask some of Toronto's problems, but don't be surprised if the lacking center rotation comes back to bite the Raptors should they reach the playoffs.

Utah Jazz
The first month revealed ... the Jaren Jackson Jr. trade looks like a mistake

No team has been more disappointing than the Jazz, who seemed ready to vault into the play-in conversation after acquiring Jackson from the Grizzlies before last season's trade deadline and drafting Darryn Peterson with the No. 2 pick. Instead, injuries to Jackson, Lauri Markkanen and Jusuf Nurkic have left Utah in the league's basement.

The Jazz's cast of young, intriguing scorers can't overcome their 23rd-ranked defense. Jackson, the planned lynchpin on that end, suffered a torn MCL in his right knee after just four games, forcing Utah to consider the broader trajectory of his career. The 27-year-old forward has played 70 games just once in the past four seasons, and his block and rebounding numbers have steadily declined since he won Defensive Player of the Year during his age-23 season with Memphis.

If Jackson can't return to form as an elite defensive anchor, the Jazz will regret taking on his significant contract and parting with three first-round picks to acquire him. Utah also traded center Walker Kessler after landing Jackson, another move that's tough to swallow given Kessler's impressive start with the Lakers.

Washington Wizards
The first month revealed ... nothing has come easily for AJ Dybantsa

The top pick in June's draft has largely been overshadowed by Yaxel Lendeborg, Cameron Boozer and Darius Acuff Jr. during the start of his rookie season. Some of that has been beyond his control: The Wizards' forward sat out the first four games because of an ankle injury and he's still finding his place on a roster that added high-usage veterans Trae Young and Anthony Davis.

But it's time to start worrying -- ever so slightly -- about Dybantsa's scoring efficiency. After leading the nation in points per game as a BYU freshman, he's averaging just 15.6 points on 40/23/71 shooting splits shooting splits. Dybantsa made his name in high school as a strong and fluid downhill attacker, but he's discovering that it's much harder to finish at the rim and earn free throws at the NBA level. He has also looked hesitant to shoot from outside.

Despite acquiring Young and encouraging center Alex Sarr to shoot more 3-pointers, the Wizards are held back by inadequate spacing. Washington ranks 27th in 3-point attempts per game and 28th in percentage. Dybantsa will keep encountering roadblocks until he has more room to operate off the dribble.

stories.headline: Fernando Alonso confirmed for Dakar Rally with Aston Martin
stories.summary: Fernando Alonso will return to the Dakar Rally in January next year as Aston Martin prepares for a surprise debut at the legendary rally raid event.
stories.body:
Fernando Alonso will return to the Dakar Rally in January next year as Aston Martin prepares for a surprise debut at the legendary rally raid event.

The Aston Martin Formula 1 driver, who last took part in the Dakar in 2020 with Toyota, will be joined in a three-car line-up by nine-time world rally champion Sebastien Loeb and world rally raid champion Lucas Moraes.

Working alongside rallying experts Prodrive, Aston Martin has produced a competition-ready rally car that has a tie-in with a military vehicle it developed for use in the video game Call of Duty, Modern Warfare 4. Known as the Dreadnought in both the virtual and real world, the rally car shares very little other than its name with its video-gaming cousin and has been designed specifically to take part in the Dakar Rally, which will return to the continent of Africa next year for the first time since 2007.

Alonso will be joined in his Dreadnought by Marc Coma -- the same co-driver he had in 2020 and a five-time Dakar motorcycle category winner.

"After deciding to continue racing in Formula One with the Aston Martin Aramco Formula One Team, I thought carefully about Dakar," Alonso, who signed a deal to race with Aston Martin in F1 in September, said.

"In the end, the decision became simple. I wanted to embrace the challenge completely and take on both Formula One and the Dakar Rally in the same year. In 2020, Dakar was one of the most challenging and enjoyable experiences of my career.

"I have enormous respect for this race and the specialists who have mastered it. Having Marc alongside me again is very important, and with Aston Martin, Prodrive, Sébastien and Lucas we have an exceptional team.

"Formula One remains my priority. But I am a racing driver, and challenges like this are why I love competing. I'm looking forward to seeing what we can achieve."

The legendary Dakar Rally was born from a series of rallies that ran from Europe to Africa in the 1970s and held its inaugural event from Paris to Dakar in 1979. Although the route changed through the two continents in the 1990s and early 2000s, the event retained its name before it eventually left Africa in 2008 due to security threats in Mauritania.

Initially the rally found a new home in South America from 2009 to 2019 before moving to Saudi Arabia in 2020, which was the event Alonso took part in and finished 13th driving for Toyota.

In October, it was announced the 2027 event would run from Portugal to Morocco due to security concerns linked to the U.S.-Israel war on Iran and deadly attacks by Yemen's Houthis on Saudi Arabia.

The event will now start in the Algarve and finish in Marrakech, stretching across 12 stages and totaling 4,341km in length. The 2027 Dakar Rally will get underway on January 9 and conclude on January 23.
